entries.question: Archer attacks with a [The Scarab God] that was turned face-down by [Ixidron] and Nia blocks with [Scathe Zombies]. Does The Scarab God trigger?
entries.reason: Both conclude the Scarab God's death trigger does not trigger because Ixidron turned it face down so it had no abilities at the relevant time.
entries.answer:
No — The Scarab God's death trigger does not trigger while it is face down.

Why: Ixidron's own text ("As this creature enters, turn all other nontoken creatures face down. (They're 2/2 creatures.)") turned The Scarab God into a face-down 2/2 with no name and no rules text. A permanent's printed characteristics, including its abilities, only come back when it is turned face up — [708.8] says that as a face-down permanent is turned face up, its copiable values revert to its normal copiable values. Until then, the object on the battlefield is not a permanent with the ability "When The Scarab God dies, return it to its owner's hand at the beginning of the next end step," so there is nothing to trigger on its death. A triggered ability needs a trigger condition on an object that actually has that ability ([603.1]).

What actually happens in combat: in the combat damage step, all assigned combat damage is dealt simultaneously and no player can act in between ([510.2], [703.4m]). The face-down 2/2 The Scarab God and the 2/2 Scathe Zombies deal 2 to each other, so both are destroyed. Any abilities that did trigger on damage being dealt are put on the stack before the active player (Archer) gets priority ([120.4b], [510.3a]). Here neither the face-down The Scarab God nor Scathe Zombies contributes such a trigger.

Timing note: if instead The Scarab God had been turned face up before combat damage was dealt, it would be a 5/5 with all its printed abilities, would survive Scathe Zombies' 2 damage, and its death trigger would work normally if it later died. And note that a face-down permanent that dies goes to the graveyard face up as its normal card, but that reveal happens after it has already left the battlefield, so it doesn't create the trigger retroactively.

One caveat on grounding: the general rule spelling out that a face-down permanent has no name, mana cost, or abilities (rule 708.2) wasn't included in my context; I'm relying on [708.8]'s statement that copiable values revert only upon being turned face up, plus Ixidron's card text. Nothing here depends on the number of players, so the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. By default, triggered abilities are checked immediately after the event in question to see if they should trigger. However, "leaves-the-battlefield" triggers check the game state immediately before the event instead. At that point, The Scarab God had no abilities.

entries.question: Aminah controls [Shapers' Sanctuary], [Spellskite], and [Feral Krushok]. Nico casts [Pyromatics] targeting Feral Krushok. Aminah activates Spellskite to change the target of Pyromatics to Spellskite. How many times does Shapers' Sanctuary trigger?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same conclusion that Shapers' Sanctuary triggers twice—once on the initial targeting and again when Spellskite becomes the spell's target—adding only a correct caveat about replicate.
entries.answer:
Twice — assuming Nico didn't pay Pyromatics' replicate cost for extra copies.

1. When Nico casts Pyromatics targeting Feral Krushok, targets are declared as part of putting the spell on the stack ([115.1]). Feral Krushok, a creature Aminah controls, becomes the target of a spell an opponent controls, so Shapers' Sanctuary triggers (Aminah may draw a card).

2. Aminah's Spellskite ability ("{U/P}: Change a target of target spell or ability to this creature") is Aminah's own ability, so Spellskite becoming the target of the Spellskite ability itself does not trigger Shapers' Sanctuary (it triggers only on spells/abilities an opponent controls). But when the Spellskite ability resolves and changes Pyromatics' target ([115.7], [115.7b], [Change a Target]), Spellskite — a creature Aminah controls — now becomes the target of Pyromatics, which is still Nico's spell. That is a second instance of a creature Aminah controls becoming the target of an opponent's spell, so Shapers' Sanctuary triggers again.

Timing notes: the Shapers' Sanctuary trigger from the initial targeting resolves before Pyromatics itself ([Shapers' Sanctuary ruling #0]), and players get priority in between, so Aminah could even use a drawn card before Pyromatics resolves ([Shapers' Sanctuary ruling #1]). Aminah's Spellskite activation happens in that window. Also note Spellskite must still be a legal target of Pyromatics when its ability resolves, or no target is changed and there's no second trigger ([Spellskite ruling #1], [Spellskite ruling #2]).

If Nico had paid replicate one or more times, each copy is a separate spell with its own target ([707.10c], and copies may have new targets chosen), so Shapers' Sanctuary would trigger once for each copy that targets a creature Aminah controls.

Player count doesn't change this: Shapers' Sanctuary cares only about whether the spell or ability is controlled by an opponent, so the count is the same at a two-player or multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Twice. Shapers' Sanctuary will trigger the first time when Pyromatics is initially cast targeting Feral Krushok.. Shapers' Sanctuary will trigger again when Spellskite becomes the target of the spell.

entries.question: Anderson plays their land for the turn, then casts a morphed [Zoetic Cavern]. Nataly casts [Delay] targeting Zoetic Cavern on the stack. After that resolves, Anderson casts [Timecrafting] to remove 2 time counters from Zoetic Cavern. After that resolves, Anderson casts Timecrafting to remove the last time counter from Zoetic Cavern. What happens to Zoetic Cavern?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude that when the last time counter is removed Anderson cannot play Zoetic Cavern because they've already played a land this turn, so it stays exiled.
entries.answer:
Zoetic Cavern stays in exile. Because Anderson already played their land for the turn, they can't play Zoetic Cavern when the suspend trigger resolves, so it simply remains exiled — now with no time counters and no longer suspended.

Step by step:

1. Anderson cast Zoetic Cavern face down using its morph ability, so on the stack it was a 2/2 face-down creature spell with no name, no text and no mana cost ([702.37c], [708.4]).
2. Nataly's Delay countered that spell and, instead of putting it into the graveyard, exiled the Zoetic Cavern card with three time counters on it and gave it suspend. "Suspended" means the card is in exile, has suspend, and has at least one time counter on it ([702.62b], [Suspend]).
3. The first Timecrafting removed 2 time counters, leaving one. Zoetic Cavern is still suspended.
4. The second Timecrafting removed the last time counter. That triggers suspend's third ability: "When the last time counter is removed from this card, if it's exiled, you may play it without paying its mana cost if able. If you don't, it remains exiled" ([702.62a]).
5. Zoetic Cavern is a land card, so "playing" it means playing it as a land, which uses Anderson's land play for the turn — and the question states Anderson already played their land this turn. So Anderson is not "able" to play it, and Zoetic Cavern remains exiled ([702.62a]). Once the last counter is gone it is no longer suspended, matching the same result described for Delay when the card can't be played ([Delay ruling #11]).

Timing note: the trigger resolves at the moment the last counter comes off, during Anderson's turn as described; it is not a delayed "next turn" permission, so the fact that the land drop is already used at that moment is what matters. If the last counter had instead been removed on a later turn on which Anderson had not yet played a land, Anderson could have played Zoetic Cavern from exile as their land for that turn.

Also note it can never come back as a face-down 2/2 this way: the suspend permission is to play it without paying its mana cost, not to pay morph's alternative cost of {3}. Its morph cost of {2} would only matter for turning it face up as a special action if it were already a face-down permanent on the battlefield ([702.37e]).

Nothing here depends on player count: the answer is the same in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table, since only Anderson (the card's owner/controller of the trigger) gets the option to play it.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: It will remain in exile. Suspend allows Anderson to play it, but does not allow Anderson to play additional lands. Since they has already played their land for the turn, they cannot play Zoetic Cavern.

entries.question: Aubree controls an [Opal Acrolith] that is currently a creature and a [Sliver Construct]. They cast [Cytoshape] to turn the Sliver Construct into a copy of Opal Acrolith. Then they activate Sliver Construct's ability to turn it into an enchantment. What happens at the end of turn?
entries.reason: Both conclude the Cytoshape copy ends at end step while the activation-created effect making it an enchantment remains, leaving a noncreature enchantment named Sliver Construct with no abilities.
entries.answer:
At end of turn, Cytoshape's copy effect wears off Sliver Construct, but the {0} ability it used while it was a copy of Opal Acrolith does NOT wear off 
b-ecause that ability's effect has no duration. So Sliver Construct ends the turn as a colorless permanent named Sliver Construct that is an Enchantment only 
u2014 not an artifact, not a creature, and with no creature types. Opal Acrolith itself is unaffected and stays a 2/4 Soldier creature.

Step by step:

1. Cytoshape resolves: Sliver Construct becomes a copy of Opal Acrolith. Copying uses copiable values, i.e. Opal Acrolith's printed characteristics 
u2014 an Enchantment with no power/toughness 
u2014 not the fact that this particular Opal Acrolith has been animated into a 2/4 Soldier creature by its own triggered ability. Cytoshape ruling #0 confirms an animated permanent is copied in its unanimated, printed form, and that Cytoshape can cause its target to stop being a creature. So Sliver Construct is now an Enchantment named Opal Acrolith with the trigger and the "{0}: This permanent becomes an enchantment" ability, and it is no longer a creature (Opal Acrolith ruling #2).

2. Aubree activates that {0} ability on Sliver Construct. It's already an enchantment, so nothing visibly changes right now unning: an ongoing type-setting effect exists with a later timestamp, applying in layer 4, and "becomes an enchantment" replaces its card types (CR 205.1a).

3. At the beginning of the end step / cleanup, Cytoshape's "until end of turn" copy effect ends and the underlying object goes back to being Sliver Construct (Cytoshape ruling #6). But the {0} ability's effect is a separate, durationless continuous effect that was created while the permanent was a copy, and effects already applying to the permanent keep applying (CR 707.4, and 700.7 / 707.11 for the effect still tracking the same object even though it changed name and characteristics). Layer resolution: base Sliver Construct (Artifact Creature 
u2014 Sliver Construct, 2/2), then layer 4 sets card types to Enchantment. Per CR 205.1a, when the creature card type is removed the correlated creature subtypes Sliver and Construct are removed too for as long as the type is gone.

Result: an Enchantment named Sliver Construct with no subtypes. Its 2/2 printed power/toughness is simply meaningless while it isn't a creature (CR 205.1a; CR 110.4c 
u2014 it stays a permanent on the battlefield). It also no longer has the Opal Acrolith abilities, since those were only copied for the turn 
u2014 so Aubree can't re-animate it, and it can't be turned back into an artifact creature by anything it has itself.

Timing note: I'm assuming the {0} activation happened after Cytoshape resolved (as stated). If instead the {0} ability had somehow been used before the copy effect began, that timestamp would be earlier than the copy and the copy would set the object's characteristics afresh anyway, and once Cytoshape ended you'd have the same layer-4 enchantment-setting effect still applying.

Multiplayer note: none of this depends on player count. The only opponent-dependent piece is Opal Acrolith's "whenever an opponent casts a creature spell" trigger, which just triggers off any opponent at a table of any size.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: The effect making Sliver Construct a copy of Opal Acrolith ends, but the effect making it an enchantment does not. It's a noncreature enchantment named "Sliver Construct" with no abilities.

entries.question: Avery controls [Bolas's Citadel] and has [Evermind] on top of their library, can they cast it?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same conclusion that Evermind can be cast with Bolas's Citadel by paying life equal to its mana value, which is 0, matching the reference.
entries.answer:
Yes — Avery can cast Evermind off the top of their library with Bolas's Citadel, paying 0 life.

Why: Bolas's Citadel says "You may play lands and cast spells from the top of your library. If you cast a spell this way, pay life equal to its mana value rather than pay its mana cost." That's an alternative cost that replaces the mana cost entirely, and it's announced as Avery proposes the spell [601.2b]. Evermind normally can't be cast because it has no mana cost and nonexistent mana costs can't be paid [202.1], but a ruling on Evermind confirms it can be cast "via some alternate means" [Evermind ruling #2] — Bolas's Citadel is exactly such a means, since Avery never needs to pay the nonexistent mana cost.

The life payment is life equal to Evermind's mana value. Evermind's mana value is 0 [Evermind ruling #3], and players can always pay 0 life [118.3b], so the cost is trivially payable regardless of Avery's life total.

One practical note: Bolas's Citadel lets Avery look at the top card any time [Bolas's Citadel ruling #3], but once Avery begins casting Evermind, the new top card can't be looked at until casting is complete [401.5, Bolas's Citadel ruling #6].

This works the same in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table; nothing about casting from the top of your library depends on the number of opponents. (Bolas's Citadel's separate sacrifice ability is the part that scales — "each opponent loses 10 life" — but that's unrelated to casting Evermind.)

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Normally because Evermind has no mana cost it can't be cast. However Bolas's Citadel is casting it for an alternative cost, and therefore ignores the actual cost of the spell. When calculating the mana value of a spell with no mana cost it's considered zero.

entries.question: Autumn controls [Bolas's Citadel] and has [Sidisi's Pet] on top of their library, can they cast it for its morph cost? If so, how much life will they pay?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Autumn cannot cast Sidisi's Pet face down using Bolas's Citadel because Bolas's Citadel and morph are both alternative costs and you cannot apply two alternative costs when casting a spell.
entries.answer:
Short answer: No — Autumn can't cast Sidisi's Pet face down off Bolas's Citadel. Bolas's Citadel's own text is an alternative cost ("If you cast a spell this way, pay life equal to its mana value rather than pay its mana cost"), and morph is also an alternative cost ("pay {3} rather than pay its mana cost"), and rule 601.2b says a player can't apply two alternative methods of casting or two alternative costs to a single spell. So Autumn must pick one, and casting from the top of the library via Bolas's Citadel forces the life payment. Casting Sidisi's Pet normally that way costs 4 life, since Sidisi's Pet's mana cost is {3}{B} (mana value 4).

Some terms: morph is a static ability that works from any zone you could cast the card from, and it lets you cast the card as a 2/2 face-down creature with no name, no subtypes and no mana cost by paying {3} instead of its mana cost (702.37a, 702.37c, 118.9b). Sidisi's Pet's printed "Morph {1}{B}" is the cost to turn the face-down permanent face up later as a special action, not a casting cost (702.37e, Sidisi's Pet ruling #5, Sidisi's Pet ruling #3).

Two notes on the legality side: casting from the top of the library is permitted for morph (702.37c lets you use morph from any zone you could normally cast the card from, and Bolas's Citadel makes the top of the library such a zone), and face-down casting legality is judged using the face-down 2/2 characteristics (601.3e, 702.37c). The blocker is purely the cost conflict, not the zone.

If Autumn instead has another way to cast Sidisi's Pet from hand, morph is fine there: pay {3}, put it on the stack face down as a 2/2, and later pay {1}{B} any time they have priority to turn it face up.

This answer is the same regardless of the number of players — nothing here depends on opponents or turn order.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No, they can't cast it. If Autumn uses Bolas's Citadel to cast a spell, they are applying an alternative cost. Morph is also an alternative cost. Only one alternative cost can be applied to a spell when casting it.

entries.question: Ashley controls [Bolas's Citadel] and has [Lovestruck Beast] on top of their library. Can they cast [Heart's Desire]? If so, how much life do they pay?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Ashley can cast the Adventure Heart's Desire from the top of the library via Bolas's Citadel and must pay life equal to that spell's mana value (1).
entries.answer:
Yes — Ashley can cast Heart's Desire from the top of their library, and they pay 1 life rather than paying {G}.

Why: Bolas's Citadel says "You may play lands and cast spells from the top of your library. If you cast a spell this way, pay life equal to its mana value rather than pay its mana cost." Because Bolas's Citadel permits casting *spells* generally (not just creature spells), the Adventure half is available. Rule 601.3e's examples make this explicit: with Melek, Izzet Paragon (instants and sorceries from the top of your library) you may cast Chop Down, the Adventure instant half of Giant Killer, but not the creature Giant Killer; with Garruk's Horde (creature spells only) the reverse is true. Bolas's Citadel allows either half, so Heart's Desire (a sorcery — Adventure) is a legal choice.

How much life: Bolas's Citadel's payment is life equal to the mana value of the spell you cast. When Ashley casts the Adventure half, the spell on the stack is Heart's Desire, whose mana cost is {G} — mana value 1. So the payment is 1 life, not 3 (3 is the mana value of the Lovestruck Beast half). This life payment is an alternative cost paid instead of the mana cost (118.9, 601.2b, 601.2f), so no mana is spent at all.

After Heart's Desire resolves, it creates a 1/1 white Human creature token and the card goes on its Adventure (exile); Ashley may later cast Lovestruck Beast from exile — but that later cast is from exile, not from the top of the library, so Bolas's Citadel's life-payment replacement does not apply to it and Lovestruck Beast would be cast for {2}{G}.

Nothing here depends on the number of players; the answer is the same in a two-player game or a multiplayer game.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes and it will cost Ashley 1 life. As part of putting Lovestruck Beast on the stack Ashley chooses whether or not they want to cast the Adventure or not. If they casts Heart's Desire they will need to pay life equal to the mana value of the spell they are casting, which in this case is one.

entries.question: Angelique has [Copy Enchantment] enter the battlefield as a copy of [Estrid's Invocation], which is a copy of [Hardened-Scale Armor]. At the beginning of their next upkeep, which permanents may Angelique exile?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same conclusion that both the Copy Enchantment (as it copied Estrid's Invocation's modified copiable values) and Estrid's Invocation itself may be exiled by their respective upkeep-triggered abilities.
entries.answer:
Angelique may exile her Copy Enchantment (now a copy of Hardened-Scale Armor that also carries the "At the beginning of your upkeep, you may exile this enchantment. If you do, return it to the battlefield under its owner's control" ability), plus the original Estrid's Invocation itself if Angelique controls it and it's her upkeep. Each ability only exiles the specific object it's on, so they are separate choices, and no other permanent (not the real Hardened-Scale Armor) can be exiled this way.

Why: when Copy Enchantment copies a permanent that is itself copying something, Copy Enchantment enters as whatever that permanent copied [Copy Enchantment ruling #6]. Estrid's Invocation's copy effect includes a modification ("except it has 'At the beginning of your upkeep...'"), and a modification made as part of a copying process becomes part of the copy's copiable values [707.9b]. So Estrid's Invocation's copiable values are "Hardened-Scale Armor with the upkeep exile ability," and Copy Enchantment picks up both the Aura text (Enchant creature; enchanted creature gets +3/+3) and the upkeep ability.

Since Copy Enchantment is an Aura copy, you chose a legal creature for it to enchant just before it entered; it must have been legally enchantable [Copy Enchantment ruling #1, 303.4d]. "This enchantment" in the granted ability refers only to that particular object, not to every permanent with the same name [201.5a] — so Angelique's copy's ability can exile only that copy, and Estrid's Invocation's own ability can exile only Estrid's Invocation.

A note on the return: whichever one Angelique exiles and returns comes back as a brand-new object with no memory of what it was [400.7, Estrid's Invocation ruling #2]. Copy Enchantment's own printed copy effect applies again as it re-enters, so Angelique again chooses any enchantment already on the battlefield to copy (or none) [Copy Enchantment ruling #7]; it can't copy something entering at the same time [Copy Enchantment ruling #2]. Any Auras attached to it are put into their owners' graveyards and counters cease to exist [Estrid's Invocation ruling #2, 704.5m].

Timing assumption: I'm reading "their next upkeep" as Angelique's own upkeep, which is what these abilities trigger on. If it were an opponent's upkeep, neither ability would trigger for Angelique. Player count doesn't change this: each such ability triggers only at its controller's upkeep, so in a multiplayer game an opposing Estrid's Invocation would give its own controller the choice on their turn, not Angelique.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold:
Since both cards will have the ability, either Copy Enchantment and Estrid's Invocation may be exiled.

The copy effect of Estrid's Invocation includes the copy gaining an ability as part of the copying process. This is also a copiable value, and Copy Enchantment will also have this ability.

entries.question: Alessandro controls [Angel's Tomb] and no other creatures. They cast [Mirage Phalanx]. Can they pair it with Angel's Tomb?
entries.reason: The candidate incorrectly asserts the soulbond trigger will be on the stack and can be ordered after Angel's Tomb's trigger, but soulbond only triggers if another eligible creature exists when Mirage Phalanx enters, so no pairing can occur.
entries.answer:
Yes — provided Alessandro puts the triggers on the stack in the right order.

Both abilities trigger when Mirage Phalanx enters: Mirage Phalanx's soulbond ability, and Angel's Tomb's ability ("Whenever a creature you control enters, you may have this artifact become a 3/3 white Angel artifact creature with flying until end of turn"). Since Alessandro controls both, they choose the order the two triggers go on the stack, so they can have Angel's Tomb's trigger resolve first.

- Angel's Tomb's trigger resolves: Alessandro has Angel's Tomb become a 3/3 white Angel artifact creature with flying until end of turn.
- Then the soulbond trigger resolves. Soulbond checks on resolution that both objects are creatures on the battlefield under the controller's control; if either isn't a creature at that time, neither becomes paired [702.95c]. Because Angel's Tomb is now a creature (and is unpaired), Mirage Phalanx and Angel's Tomb become paired [702.95b], and each then has the token-copying ability granted by Mirage Phalanx.

If instead the soulbond trigger resolves first, Angel's Tomb is still just a noncreature artifact at that moment, so there is no other unpaired creature and no pairing happens [702.95c]; the later Angel's Tomb trigger doesn't retroactively create a pairing. Note also that a creature can be paired with only one other creature [702.95d], and Mirage Phalanx's own text keeps them paired only for as long as Alessandro controls both.

This answer doesn't depend on the number of players at the table; nothing here involves other players' choices.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Soulbond is a triggered ability that will only go on the stack if Alessandro controls another eligible creature when Mirage Phalanx enters the battlefield. However, before Angel's Tomb's ability resolves, Alessandro doesn't control any other eligible creatures.

entries.question: Ariyah controls [The Ozolith] and [Putrid Goblin] with a -1/-1 counter on it. What happens if Putrid Goblin dies?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Putrid Goblin stays in the graveyard (persist doesn't trigger because it had a -1/-1 counter on it) and The Ozolith receives a -1/-1 counter matching the Goblin's.
entries.answer:
Putrid Goblin stays in the graveyard — its persist ability does not trigger, because Putrid Goblin already had a -1/-1 counter on it when it died — and The Ozolith's first ability triggers and puts one -1/-1 counter on The Ozolith.

Details:

1. Persist reads "When this creature dies, if it had no -1/-1 counters on it, return it to the battlefield... with a -1/-1 counter on it." Since Putrid Goblin had a -1/-1 counter on it as it left the battlefield, the intervening-"if" condition fails and persist doesn't trigger. (If instead Putrid Goblin had also had a +1/+1 counter, the state-based action in [704.5q]/[122.3] would have removed one of each, leaving no -1/-1 counter, and persist could return it — see [Putrid Goblin ruling #0]. That's not the case here.)

2. The Ozolith's ability, "Whenever a creature you control leaves the battlefield, if it had counters on it, put those counters on The Ozolith," triggers. It does not physically move the counter off the dead Putrid Goblin — the counter on Putrid Goblin simply ceases to exist when the card changes zones ([122.2], [400.7]). Instead Ariyah puts the same number and kind of counters Putrid Goblin had onto The Ozolith, i.e. one -1/-1 counter ([122.8], [The Ozolith ruling #3]).

3. Importantly, The Ozolith's ability resolving first does not "clean" Putrid Goblin's counter for persist's purposes: an ability that checks the counters a creature had as it left the battlefield uses the counters that were on it on the battlefield ([The Ozolith ruling #3]).

4. Afterward, at the beginning of combat on Ariyah's turn, The Ozolith's second ability may move all counters from The Ozolith onto a target creature — here that would dump a -1/-1 counter onto that creature, so Ariyah may prefer not to (the ability says "you may"). If the target is illegal on resolution, no counters leave The Ozolith ([The Ozolith ruling #5]); if The Ozolith itself leaves the battlefield first, no counters move ([The Ozolith ruling #2]).

This result is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table; nothing here depends on the number of opponents.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Putrid Goblin will not return to the battlefield. The Ozolith will have a -1/-1 counter put on it. The Ozolith's ability does not remove counters from the creature, it just puts counters on The Ozolith matching the number and types of counters that the creature had on it when it died. Persist will look back in time to determine if Putrid Goblin had a -1/-1 counter on it at the time it died. Since it did, persist will not trigger.

entries.question: Ares controls [Majestic Auricorn] merged with [Orochi Eggwatcher] on top. They cause Orochi Eggwatcher to flip. What happens?
entries.reason: Both say the merged permanent flips and uses Orochi Eggwatcher's flipped characteristics while Majestic Auricorn (a nonflip component) continues to contribute its abilities, so the core ruling is identical.
entries.answer:
The whole merged permanent becomes flipped, and because Orochi Eggwatcher is the top component, the merged permanent now uses Shidako, Broodmistress's alternative characteristics: it's a legendary Snake Shaman named Shidako, Broodmistress, 3/3, with "{G}, Sacrifice a creature: Target creature gets +3/+3 until end of turn" — plus all abilities from the component underneath it (Majestic Auricorn's vigilance and "Whenever this creature mutates, you gain 4 life").

Details:
- "Flipped" is one of the four status categories a permanent always has (tapped/untapped, flipped/unflipped, face up/face down, phased in/phased out) [110.5]. Flipping a permanent means turning it 180° so a flip card's upside-down alternative name, type line, text box, and power/toughness apply instead of its normal ones [710.1, 710.2].
- A merged permanent is a single permanent represented by multiple components. When a merged permanent contains a flip card, that component's alternative characteristics are used instead of its normal characteristics while the merged permanent is flipped [730.2h]. Since Orochi Eggwatcher is the top component, its alternative face (Shidako, Broodmistress) supplies the merged permanent's name, types, text box, and power/toughness, while Majestic Auricorn underneath continues to contribute only its abilities (that's how mutate works: the creature on top plus all abilities from under it).
- The flip is triggered by Orochi Eggwatcher's own activated ability, so it only actually flips if Ares controls ten or more creatures when that ability resolves; otherwise the token is created and nothing flips.
- This is one-way: once flipped, the permanent can't become unflipped [710.4]. If it later leaves the battlefield, one permanent leaves and both cards (Majestic Auricorn and the Orochi Eggwatcher flip card) go to the appropriate zone, with no memory of flipped status [730.3, 710.4].

Nothing here depends on the number of players, so the answer is the same in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: The merged permanent will flip. The merged permanent will now use Orochi Eggwatcher's flip-side alternate characteristics. This will not affect any abilities the merged permanent has because of Majestic Auricorn, since that component is not a flip card.

entries.question: Nico controls [Vedalken Orrery]. Axl casts [Warrior's Oath]. After it resolves, Nico casts [Trouble in Pairs]. Axl passes the turn. Who takes the next turn?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Trouble in Pairs is on the battlefield when Axl's extra turn would begin, so Axl's extra turn is skipped and Nico (the next player) takes the next turn.
entries.answer:
Axl skips the extra turn, so the next turn belongs to the next player in turn order — Nico in a two-player game.

Why: Warrior's Oath gave Axl an extra turn after the current one. Trouble in Pairs says "If an opponent would begin an extra turn, that player skips that turn instead." entries.question: Amaris controls a [The Flame of Keld] with 2 lore counters on it and [Soul-Scar Mage]. entries.question: Aspen attacks with [Aurelia, the Warleader]. Immediately after the trigger resolves, they casts [Time Stop]. Is there an additional combat phase? If so, when?

Why: Aurelia, the Warleader's trigger, when it resolved, untapped all creatures Aspen controls and added an additional combat phase directly after the current combat phase (rule 500.8 — extra phases are inserted after the specified phase). But when Time Stop resolves it "ends the turn": all other spells and abilities on the stack are exiled, all attacking and blocking creatures are removed from combat, the current phase and step end, and the game skips straight to the cleanup step, skipping any phases or steps in between (rule 724.1d; Time Stop ruling #3). The additional combat phase created by Aurelia, the Warleader sits between the current combat phase and the cleanup step, so it is one of the phases skipped. Skipping a phase means proceeding past it as though it didn't exist (rules 500.11, 614.10b), and a skipped phase is not saved for later — it is simply gone for that turn. Note also that Aurelia, the Warleader grants no additional main phase (Aurelia, the Warleader ruling #0), so nothing else survives either.

Timing assumption: you said Time Stop was cast immediately after Aurelia, the Warleader's trigger resolved, i.e., during the declare attackers step of the first combat phase, with the extra combat phase already scheduled. If instead Time Stop had resolved before Aurelia, the Warleader's trigger resolved, the trigger would have been exiled off the stack and the extra combat phase would never have been created at all — same practical result: no additional combat.

This analysis doesn't depend on the number of players; it works identically in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table, since ending the turn affects the turn structure itself.

entries.answer_gold: There is no additional combat phase. When Aurelia, the Warleader's trigger resolves, it adds the phase to the structure of the current turn. When Time Stop resolves, it skips all remaining steps and phases until the cleanup step.

entries.question: In Aspen's draw step, they tap [Vault of Catlacan] for 8 blue mana and cast [Time Stop]. Aspen discards a [Guile] to hand size. Can they use the two remaining {U} to cast an instant?

Direct answer: Yes — Aspen does get a window to cast an instant, because discarding Guile creates a triggered ability. But the two floating {U} are almost certainly gone by then, so with only that mana available they can't pay for it.

Why there's a window: Time Stop ends the turn. When an effect ends the turn, no player gets priority during that process and triggered abilities are not put onto the stack [724.1f]. Guile's own text — "When Guile is put into a graveyard from anywhere, shuffle it into its owner's library" — triggers when Aspen discards it to hand size during the end-the-turn process. Because at least one triggered ability has triggered since the process began, that ability is put onto the stack during the cleanup step, then the active player (Aspen) gets priority and players may cast spells and activate abilities; another cleanup step follows before the turn actually ends [724.1f], [514.3a]. Without any such trigger, no player would get priority at all in the cleanup step [514.3], [514.3a].

Why the mana is the problem: the two remaining {U} were produced in the draw step. The rule governing mana pools emptying at the end of each step and phase was not included in the context I was given, so I can't cite it — but nothing in the provided rules keeps mana alive across the change of step/phase, and no game events occur between steps or phases [500.12]. Practically, Aspen would need to produce mana anew during that cleanup‑step priority window (Vault of Catlacan is already tapped), or the instant must cost nothing. Note also that mana abilities can't be activated at all while Time Stop is resolving except as an effect instructs [608.2g].

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Time Stop resolved fully and the hand-size discard happened as part of the end-the-turn process, which is when Guile's shuffle trigger triggers. If instead Guile had somehow reached the graveyard before Time Stop began resolving, that trigger would have been exiled along with everything else on the stack, no ability would be waiting, and there would be no priority window in the cleanup step at all [724.1f].

This analysis is the same regardless of the number of players; the only player who gets priority first in that cleanup window is the active player, Aspen [724.1f], [117.1].

entries.question: Alex controls an [Oracle of Mul Daya] and has played 2 lands this turn. They casts [Flicker], targeting the Oracle of Mul Daya. After if resolves, can they play a 3rd land?

No. Alex still can play only 2 lands this turn, and they have already played 2.

Why: Oracle of Mul Daya's first ability ("You may play an additional land on each of your turns") is a static ability generating a continuous effect. Such an effect isn't "locked in" — it applies at any given moment to whatever its text indicates [611.3a]. So the permission is measured right now, not accumulated. With one Oracle of Mul Daya on the battlefield, Alex's limit is one normal land play plus one additional = 2.

To see whether a land play is legal, you compare the number of lands the player can play this turn against the number they have already played this turn; the play is legal only if the first number is greater [305.2a]. If the number they can play is equal to or less than the number already played, they can't play a land for any reason [305.2b]. Alex can play 2 and has played 2, so no third land play.

Flicker exiles the Oracle of Mul Daya and returns it, and the returned permanent is a brand-new object with no memory of its previous existence [400.7i] — but that only matters for the object's own identity, not for Alex's record of lands played this turn, which is tracked per player and is not reset. And since there is still just one Oracle of Mul Daya on the battlefield, the additional-land permission is still just one. (Two copies would stack to 3 land plays [Oracle of Mul Daya ruling #0], but flickering one copy doesn't create a second instance.)

Also note the permission only ever expands the count of lands playable — Alex would still need priority, an empty stack, and their own main phase to play a land [305.1], [116.2a], and playing a land from the top of the library still counts as one of the turn's land plays [Oracle of Mul Daya ruling #2].

Timing assumption: I'm assuming both lands were played before Flicker resolved and that Alex asks after Flicker has finished resolving. If instead Alex had played only 1 land at that point, they could still play a second (not a third) land afterward. Nothing here depends on player count, so the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

entries.question: Nathaniel controls [Pithing Needle] naming [Skullsnatcher]. Alex has Skullsnatcher in their hand and declares an attack with [Borderland Minotaur]. Nathaniel declares no blockers. Can Alex use ninjutsu to put Skullsnatcher onto the battlefield?

entries.question: Ari attacks with [Suntail Hawk]. Nayeli casts [Vault Skyward] to give [Brimaz, King of Oreskos] flying until end of turn and blocks Suntail Hawk. Will the token created by Brimaz, King of Oreskos also be blocking Suntail Hawk?
entries.reason: Both say yes—the token enters the battlefield already blocking Suntail Hawk because creatures put onto the battlefield blocking aren’t subject to blocker-declaration restrictions and Brimaz’s triggered ability specifies the creature it’s blocking.
entries.answer:
Yes. Brimaz, King of Oreskos's triggered ability ("Whenever Brimaz blocks a creature, create a 1/1 white Cat Soldier creature token with vigilance that's blocking that creature") creates the token already blocking Suntail Hawk, even though Suntail Hawk has flying and the token does not.

Why: a creature put onto the battlefield blocking isn't affected by the requirements or restrictions that apply to the declaration of blockers [509.4b], and flying is exactly such a restriction on declaring blockers. Because Brimaz, King of Oreskos's ability specifies what the token is blocking, its controller doesn't choose a different creature [509.4]. So the token enters the battlefield blocking Suntail Hawk.

Timing assumption: Nayeli cast Vault Skyward before the declare blockers step so Brimaz, King of Oreskos could legally be declared as a blocker for Suntail Hawk, and Brimaz, King of Oreskos was in fact declared as a blocker — that declaration is what triggers its ability [509.1g, 509.3b]. The trigger goes on the stack and resolves before the active player gets priority in the declare blockers step [509.2a], so the token appears then. If instead Vault Skyward were cast after blockers were declared, giving flying wouldn't retroactively let Brimaz, King of Oreskos block [Vault Skyward ruling #1], and with no legal block there'd be no trigger and no token.

Two caveats about the token: it is "blocking" but for trigger events and effects it never "blocked," so abilities that trigger on a creature blocking won't trigger from it [509.4, Brimaz, King of Oreskos ruling #2]. Also, since Nayeli is a defending player against Suntail Hawk, which is still attacking, the token is validly a blocking creature; if Suntail Hawk had been removed from combat first, the token would enter but never be considered blocking [509.4a, 506.3e].

This works the same whether the game has two players or more; the only multiplayer wrinkle in the provided rules is that the token's controller must be a defending player for the attacking creature named [509.4a].

entries.answer_gold: Yes. The only time the game checks to see if the declaration of blockers is illegal is as Nayeli declares blockers. A creature that's put onto the battlefield blocking isn't declared as a blocker and isn't affected by requirements or restrictions that normally alter what a player is allowed to declare as a blocker.

entries.question: Aryan splice [Evermind] onto [Barrel Down Sokenzan]. Can they target [Phyrexian Crusader] with the spliced spell?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude you cannot target Phyrexian Crusader because splicing Evermind adds only its text, not its blue color, leaving the spell red and unable to target a creature with protection from red.
entries.answer:
No. The spliced spell is still Barrel Down Sokenzan — a red instant — so Phyrexian Crusader's "protection from red and from white" prevents it from being chosen as a target.

Why: Splice is a static ability that works from your hand; revealing Evermind as you cast an Arcane spell adds only Evermind's rules text ("Draw a card") to Barrel Down Sokenzan and costs an additional {1}{U} [702.47a]. The resulting spell keeps all of Barrel Down Sokenzan's own characteristics — name, mana cost {2}{R}, and color red; it gains none of Evermind's characteristics, including Evermind's blue color [702.47c, 612.10]. Splice is purely a text-changing effect [612.1].

Because the spell is red, and Phyrexian Crusader has protection from red, Phyrexian Crusader can't be targeted by it [702.16b]. Note protection from red and from white behaves as two separate protection abilities [702.16i]. Targets are chosen normally after you reveal the spliced card [702.47d, 601.2c, Evermind ruling #5], but you must choose a legal target — Phyrexian Crusader isn't one, so if it's your only creature option, you can't legally cast the spliced spell targeting it. Even if it somehow became a target and then gained protection later, the spell would check targets on resolution and be countered for having no legal targets [608.2b].

Also note: Evermind's added text contains no instance of "target," so splicing it doesn't give you an extra, protection-immune target to work with; it only adds "Draw a card." (Contrast the Glacial Ray example, where the added damage text is treated as coming from the main spell and so uses the main spell's color [702.47c, 201.5b].)

This answer doesn't depend on player count — it's the same in a two-player or multiplayer game, since protection here is based on the spell's color, not on who controls it.

entries.answer_gold: No. Evermind has a color indicator that makes it blue, and that will not be spliced onto Barrel Down Sokenzan because it's not a part of its text box.

entries.question: Armani controls [Soul Echo] with 0 counters on it and Nico controls [Spirit of the Hearth]. Will Armani have to sacrifice Soul Echo at the beginning of their upkeep?
entries.reason: Both conclude that the upkeep ability requires a target and, with Nico's hexproof leaving no legal target, the ability can't be put on the stack and Soul Echo is not sacrificed.
entries.answer:
Direct answer: If Nico is Armani's only opponent, Armani does not sacrifice Soul Echo — the triggered ability has no legal target and never resolves, so the "sacrifice this enchantment" instruction is never carried out. If there is at least one other opponent at the table who doesn't have hexproof, Armani must target that opponent, the ability resolves, and Soul Echo is sacrificed (because there are no echo counters on it).

Why: Soul Echo's upkeep ability reads "At the beginning of your upkeep, sacrifice this enchantment if there are no echo counters on it. Otherwise, target opponent may choose..." The word "target opponent" is part of the ability, so the ability requires a target opponent to be chosen when it's put on the stack, even though the sacrifice clause itself doesn't use the target. Spirit of the Hearth says "You have hexproof," so Nico can't be the target of spells or abilities Armani controls.

Two-player vs. multiplayer: in a two-player game (Nico the only opponent) there is no legal opponent to target, so the ability can't be put on the stack legally / is removed for having no legal target and Soul Echo survives with 0 counters. At a multiplayer table, any other opponent is a legal target, the ability resolves, and Soul Echo is sacrificed.

Caveat on grounding: the numbered rules supplied here cover state-based actions and counters (e.g., [704.1], [117.5]) but do not include the targeting rules about abilities with no legal targets being removed from the stack. That part of the answer follows from Soul Echo's and Spirit of the Hearth's own printed text ("target opponent" plus "You have hexproof") rather than from a rule quoted above. Note also that the sacrifice here is an ordinary resolution of a triggered ability, not a state-based action, so it does not happen automatically the way, say, a 0-loyalty planeswalker or 0-defense battle is put into the graveyard ([122.1e], [122.1g], [704.1]).

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Since the ability has no legal targets, it would trigger at the beginning of the upkeep but would not be put on the stack.

entries.question: Addison controls [The Book of Vile Darkness], and token copies of [Eye of Vecna] and [Hand of Vecna] created by [Saheeli's Artistry]. Addison then activates The Book of Vile Darkness. What abilities will the Vecna token have?
entries.reason: The candidate says Vecna has indestructible and "no other abilities," but the reference states Vecna also has the Book-defined end-step trigger (create a 2/2 Zombie if you lost 2+ life), so the conclusions differ.
entries.answer:
Vecna will be a legendary 8/8 black Zombie God token with indestructible and no other abilities — it gains no triggered abilities from the exiled token copies.

Why: Saheeli's Artistry creates tokens that are copies of Eye of Vecna and Hand of Vecna, and a copy's name is a copiable value, so those tokens really are named Eye of Vecna and Hand of Vecna ([707.2], [707.2a], [111.4] — see the Spitting Image/Doomed Dissenter example). They're also artifacts you control, so they legally pay the cost of The Book of Vile Darkness's ability: "{T}, Exile The Book of Vile Darkness and artifacts you control named Eye of Vecna and Hand of Vecna."

But the ability then grants "all triggered abilities of the exiled cards," and the official ruling spells out that this ability looks at the *cards* in exile, not the permanents that were on the battlefield ([The Book of Vile Darkness ruling #2]). Token copies are not cards, so once they're exiled there are no Eye of Vecna or Hand of Vecna cards in exile for Vecna to copy abilities from. Vecna therefore enters with only the characteristics The Book of Vile Darkness itself defines: legendary, 8/8, black, Zombie God, indestructible ([111.3] — a token has no characteristics beyond those defined by the ability that created it).

Consequences of that: Vecna gets no Eye of Vecna enters-the-battlefield trigger (no card draw, no 2 life lost) even though such gained triggers would normally be copiable and would trigger ([The Book of Vile Darkness ruling #0]), and no Hand of Vecna beginning-of-combat +X/+X trigger. Contrast the normal case, where the real cards are exiled and Vecna gains the one trigger from Hand of Vecna and the two from Eye of Vecna ([The Book of Vile Darkness ruling #1]).

This answer doesn't depend on the number of players; nothing here involves opponents or defending players.

Timing note: I'm assuming the token copies were the objects exiled to pay the cost. If Addison also controlled the actual Eye of Vecna and/or Hand of Vecna cards and exiled those instead (or in addition), Vecna would gain the triggered abilities of whichever real cards ended up in exile.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Only indestructible and "At the beginning of your end step, if you lost 2 or more life this turn, create a 2/2 black Zombie creature token.". It won't get the abilities of the exiled tokens, because they're not cards.

entries.question: Aspen casts [Buried Alive] while controlling [Extus, Oriq Overlord]. Can they put [Virulent Sliver] into their graveyard with Buried Alive, and return it with Extus, Oriq Overlord's triggered ability?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Extus's triggered ability triggers on casting and must pick a target before Buried Alive resolves, so it cannot target the Virulent Sliver that Buried Alive will put into the graveyard.
entries.answer:
No — not the same Virulent Sliver put there by that same Buried Alive. Aspen can put Virulent Sliver into the graveyard with Buried Alive, but Extus, Oriq Overlord's Magecraft ability triggers when Buried Alive is *cast*, so the trigger goes on the stack (and its target is chosen) above Buried Alive, while Virulent Sliver is still in Aspen's library. There is no legal target among cards Buried Alive hasn't put into the graveyard yet, so Magecraft must target some other nonlegendary creature card already in Aspen's graveyard; if there is none, the trigger is removed from the stack for having no legal target. The Magecraft trigger then resolves before Buried Alive does.

So the sequence is: cast Buried Alive → Magecraft triggers and picks a target from cards already in the graveyard → Magecraft resolves → Buried Alive resolves, searching up to three creature cards (Virulent Sliver among them) into the graveyard and shuffling.

Virulent Sliver is a nonlegendary creature card, so it is a fine Magecraft target later — with a subsequent instant or sorcery cast or copied, Extus, Oriq Overlord's Magecraft can return Virulent Sliver from the graveyard to Aspen's hand.

Nothing here depends on the number of players; the answer is the same in two-player and multiplayer games.

entries.answer_gold: No. Extus, Oriq Overlord triggers when Aspen casts Buried Alive, and will go on the stack above it. At this point, a legal target has to be chosen. The ability will then resolve before the spell that caused it to trigger does.

entries.question: Aiyana casts [Murktide Regent], exiling 5 instants. In response, Nico casts [Dress Down]. How many +1/+1 counters will Murktide Regent enter the battlefield with?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Murktide Regent enters with zero +1/+1 counters because Dress Down resolves first and removes its abilities, so the enters-with-counters replacement effect doesn't apply.
entries.answer:
Murktide Regent enters the battlefield with zero +1/+1 counters — a plain 3/3 with no flying while Dress Down remains on the battlefield.

Why: Dress Down was cast in response to Murktide Regent, so Dress Down is on top of the stack and resolves first (rule 117.7, 608.1). Once Dress Down has resolved, its static ability "Creatures lose all abilities" is a continuous effect already in existence.

"This creature enters with a +1/+1 counter on it for each instant and sorcery card exiled with it" is a replacement effect that modifies how Murktide Regent enters the battlefield (rule 614.1c). To determine whether such an effect applies, you check the characteristics of the permanent as it would exist on the battlefield, taking into account continuous effects that already exist and would apply to it (rule 614.12a). Continuous effects that modify a permanent's characteristics apply simultaneously with it entering, not afterward (rule 611.3c). Because Dress Down's effect strips Murktide Regent of all abilities as it enters, Murktide Regent no longer has the enters-with-counters ability, and no counters are placed. It also has no flying and no "whenever an instant or sorcery card leaves your graveyard" trigger while Dress Down is out.

Note on the cost: delve let Aiyana exile 5 instants to pay for {5} of the cost, so the remaining cost paid was {U}{U}. Delve doesn't change the spell's mana cost or mana value — Murktide Regent's mana value is still 7 (Murktide Regent ruling #0).

Timing caveat: this assumes Dress Down resolved before Murktide Regent resolved, which is what "in response" means. If instead Dress Down were cast and resolved only after Murktide Regent had already entered with 5 counters, those counters would stay on it (counters aren't abilities) — Murktide Regent would be a 3/3 with five +1/+1 counters (8/8) but with no abilities; a replacement effect can't go back in time to undo an event that already happened (rule 614.4).

This analysis doesn't depend on the number of players: it works the same at a two-player table or in multiplayer, since only the caster's own permanent and Dress Down's global effect are involved.

entries.answer_gold: Zero. When determining how to apply Murktide Regent's replacement effect, its characteristics are checked as it would exist on the battlefield. Since Dress Down is on the battlefield, Murktide Regent would have no abilities while on the battlefield, so its replacement effect won't apply.

entries.question: Nathaniel controls [Dryad Militant]. Armani casts [Hanabi Blast]. Does it return to their hand?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same conclusion as the reference—Hanabi Blast returns to its owner's hand as part of its resolution and thus never goes to the graveyard for Dryad Militant's replacement effect to apply.
entries.answer:
Yes. Hanabi Blast returns to its owner's hand as normal; Nathaniel's Dryad Militant doesn't stop it.

Dryad Militant's ability only replaces an event where an instant or sorcery card would be put into a graveyard from anywhere — it exiles the card instead. Hanabi Blast's own text moves it from the stack to its owner's hand during resolution, so it never goes to a graveyard and Dryad Militant's replacement effect never applies.

A few details:
- It goes to its *owner's* hand, not necessarily the caster's. If Armani cast a Hanabi Blast owned by someone else, it returns to that owner's hand and Armani still discards a card at random ([Hanabi Blast ruling #0]). Rule [400.3] likewise sends a card to its owner's hand rather than another player's.
- The random discard afterward: if the discarded card happens to be an instant or sorcery, Dryad Militant exiles it instead of letting it reach the graveyard, though discard-triggered abilities (like madness) still function and effects that look at the discarded card can find it in exile ([Dryad Militant ruling #0]).
- If Hanabi Blast is countered, or is otherwise put into a graveyard rather than resolving, then Dryad Militant does apply and it is exiled instead.

This works the same regardless of how many players are at the table; ownership, not the number of opponents, is what matters here.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Resolving spells do not leave the stack until they finish resolving. Returning the Hanabi Blast to its owner's hand is part of its resolution, so it is never put into exile.

entries.question: In a two-player game, Ally casts [Rushblade Commander]. Can they attack with it this turn?
entries.reason: Both conclude that Rushblade Commander grants haste to itself (in a two-player game "your team" is just you), so it can attack the turn it enters.
entries.answer:
Yes. Rushblade Commander can attack the turn it comes down, because it gives itself haste.

Rushblade Commander is a Creature — Azra Warrior, and its ability reads "Warriors your team controls have haste." Since Rushblade Commander is itself a Warrior its controller (Ally, or Ally's team) controls, Rushblade Commander grants haste to itself. This is card text applying to itself; it isn't an exception to a general rule so much as a static ability that turns on immediately on the battlefield.

Normally rule 302.6 — the informal "summoning sickness" rule — says a creature can't attack unless it has been under its controller's control continuously since the beginning of their most recent turn, and rule 508.1a repeats that each declared attacker must be untapped and either have haste or have been controlled continuously since the turn began. Haste specifically waives that: rule 702.10b lets a creature attack even if it hasn't been controlled continuously since its controller's most recent turn began. So Rushblade Commander qualifies under the "or have haste" clause of 508.1a.

Two further notes: Rushblade Commander must still be untapped when attackers are declared (508.1a), and Ally must still be in a turn where they're the active player and reach the declare attackers step. Also, rule 702.10c means Ally could activate {T} or {Q} abilities of any Warrior they control right away, though Rushblade Commander as printed has none.

Your question specifies two players, so "your team" is simply Ally alone. At a multiplayer table using teams (the wording "your team" is aimed at team formats), the haste would extend to Warriors Ally's teammates control as well; the provided rules don't cover team-format details beyond that, so treat the two-player reading as the answer here.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. In a two-player game, "your team" means "you".

entries.question: Alberto casts [Parch] with its second mode, targeting Nico's [Kasimir the Lone Wolf]. In response, Nico casts [Prismatic Lace], choosing red. What happens when Parch resolves?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude that Prismatic Lace makes Kasimir no longer blue, so Parch has an illegal target at resolution and is removed from the stack without dealing damage.
entries.answer:
Parch is countered on resolution for having an illegal target — Kasimir the Lone Wolf takes no damage.

Why: Alberto chose Parch's second mode, "Parch deals 4 damage to target blue creature," so the target must be a blue creature. Prismatic Lace says "Target permanent becomes the color or colors of your choice," and Nico chose red — that replaces Kasimir the Lone Wolf's colors entirely, so Kasimir the Lone Wolf is now red and not blue. This color change lasts indefinitely, not just while Prismatic Lace is resolving.

When Parch tries to resolve, it rechecks whether its target is still legal; a target whose characteristics have changed so it no longer matches the targeting requirement is illegal. Since Parch's only target is now illegal, Parch doesn't resolve at all — it's removed from the stack and put into Alberto's graveyard, and no damage is dealt (see [608.2b]).

Alberto also can't switch to the first mode ("Parch deals 2 damage to any target") to save the spell; modes are locked in when the spell is cast, and nothing here offers a chance to change them.

This outcome is the same whether the game has two players or more, since only Alberto's spell and Nico's permanent are involved. If instead Prismatic Lace had chosen colors including blue (for example, blue and red), Kasimir the Lone Wolf would still be a legal blue creature and Parch would deal 4 damage normally.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: The Kasimir the Lone Wolf is now a mono-red permanent; it is no longer blue. The game checks to see if its targets are still legal. Kasimir the Lone Wolf is no longer a legal target for Parch, so it is removed from the stack and doesn't resolve.

entries.question: Alfonso has 20 life and has cast a [Channel] previously this turn. Nancy casts [Word of Command], choosing [Squire] from Alfonso's hand. Can Nancy have Alfonso pay 20 life to add 20 colorless mana while casting the Squire, causing Alfonso to lose the game?
entries.reason: The candidate incorrectly concludes Channel is blocked by Word of Command, while the reference correctly states Channel is a special action (not a mana ability) and therefore may be used to pay life for colorless mana while casting Squire.
entries.answer:
No. While Nancy controls Alfonso under Word of Command, Word of Command's own text says the controlled player "can activate mana abilities only if they're from lands that player controls and only if mana they produce is spent to activate other mana abilities of lands the player controls and/or to play that card." Channel's effect is not a mana ability of a land Alfonso controls — it's a floating effect from a resolved sorcery that lets him pay 1 life for {C} any time he could activate a mana ability — so Nancy cannot use it at all during the Word of Command play. This card-specific restriction overrides the general rule (723.5a) that a controller may otherwise freely use the controlled player's resources to pay costs.

Two further points, had the restriction not existed:
- Squire costs {1}{W}. The {W} must be white mana, which Channel's {C} can never pay; {C} is colorless specifically and only the {1} generic portion could be paid with it (202.1). So Channel mana alone can't even cast Squire.
- Under Word of Command, mana produced must be spent on that card or on other land mana abilities, so making 20 extra {C} "for nothing" isn't a legal use.

On the life question itself: paying 20 life at exactly 20 life would be legal in the abstract, since a player may pay life only if their life total is at least the payment (119.4, 118.3), and Alfonso would then be at 0 and lose the game the next time a player would receive priority (119.6, 104.3b). But per Channel ruling #0, once at 0 he could not pay any further life. That path just isn't available here because of Word of Command's mana-ability restriction.

This analysis doesn't depend on player count — Word of Command targets one opponent, so it reads the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. There is no restriction on how much mana Alfonso can add while casting Squire. While Word of Command does prevent Alfonso from activating mana abilities that aren't used to cast Squire, paying 1 life to add {C} due to Channel is not a mana ability, it is a special action.

entries.question: Aimee casts [Animate Dead] targeting [Scalebane's Elite] in their graveyard. What happens?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Animate Dead can't attach to the returned Scalebane's Elite (due to protection), so Animate Dead ends up in the graveyard and its leaves-the-battlefield trigger causes Scalebane's Elite to be sacrificed.
entries.answer:
Scalebane's Elite comes back to the battlefield under Aimee's control, but Animate Dead can't attach to it (protection from black), so Animate Dead goes to Aimee's graveyard as a state-based action, and its leaves-the-battlefield delayed trigger then makes Aimee sacrifice Scalebane's Elite.

Step by step:

1. Animate Dead targets the Scalebane's Elite card in the graveyard; protection from black doesn't stop this, because protection functions only on the battlefield ([Animate Dead ruling #4]). Animate Dead resolves and enters the battlefield attached to that card in the graveyard ([608.3c], [Animate Dead ruling #1]).
2. Animate Dead's enters trigger resolves: it loses "enchant creature card in a graveyard," gains "enchant creature put onto the battlefield with this Aura," returns Scalebane's Elite to the battlefield under Aimee's control, and tries to attach itself to Scalebane's Elite.
3. Now Scalebane's Elite is on the battlefield with protection from black, and Animate Dead is a black Aura, so it can't legally enchant Scalebane's Elite. The attach attempt fails and Animate Dead doesn't move onto it ([701.3b], [303.4j]).
4. Animate Dead is therefore attached to nothing (its old graveyard object no longer exists), so the state-based action puts Animate Dead into Aimee's graveyard ([704.5m], [303.4c], [704.1]).
5. Animate Dead leaving the battlefield triggers its delayed ability "When this Aura leaves the battlefield, that creature's controller sacrifices it." When that trigger resolves, if Scalebane's Elite is still on the battlefield, Aimee sacrifices it ([Animate Dead ruling #0]).

Net result: Aimee spent {1}{B}, Animate Dead ends up in the graveyard, and Scalebane's Elite gets sacrificed (unless something removes it or the trigger first). Note Animate Dead's printed text overrides normal Aura behavior in one respect: it enters attached to a card in a graveyard rather than a battlefield permanent.

This interaction is entirely between Aimee's own cards, so the answer is the same whether the game has two players or more.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold:
Both permanents end up in the graveyard.

Scalebane's Elite's protection ability doesn't function in the graveyard, so it's a legal target for Animate Dead. As Animate Dead's trigger resolves, first Animate Dead's enchant ability changes to "enchant creature put onto the battlefield with Animate Dead". Then Scalebane's Elite is returned to the battlefield. At this point the next instruction is to attach Animate Dead to Scalebane's Elite, but this is illegal to do because now that it's on the battlefield, Scalebane's Elite's protection ability is active.

After the triggered ability from Animate Dead has finished resolving, the game will check state-based actions and see that Animate Dead is an Aura that isn't enchanting anything, so it's put into its owner's graveyard.. This causes Animate Dead's leaves-the-battlefield ability to trigger, sacrificing Scalebane's Elite.

entries.question: Alondra controls an [Invasion of Ixalan] with 1 defense counter on it. They attack it with [Rankle and Torbran]. If they choose the second mode for Rankle and Torbran's triggered ability, could they sacrifice Invasion of Ixalan's back face [Belligerent Regisaur] to it?
entries.reason: The candidate concludes Alondra cannot sacrifice Belligerent Regisaur, but the correct ruling is that Alondra can order triggers so Invasion of Ixalan's trigger resolves first, creating Belligerent Regisaur before Rankle and Torbran's ability resolves, allowing it to be sacrificed.
entries.answer:
No. Alondra cannot sacrifice Belligerent Regisaur to Rankle and Torbran's second mode, for two independent reasons.

1) Timing. Rankle and Torbran's combat damage trigger and Invasion of Ixalan's "when it's defeated" trigger both go on the stack at the same time; the sacrifice happens while Rankle and Torbran's ability is resolving. Invasion of Ixalan's defeated trigger hasn't resolved yet, so it hasn't been exiled and cast transformed, and Belligerent Regisaur is not yet a permanent on the battlefield. A player can only sacrifice a permanent they control on the battlefield ([701.21a]), so there is nothing named Belligerent Regisaur to sacrifice at that moment. (Note also that having defense 0 doesn't immediately bin Invasion of Ixalan, because it is the source of a triggered ability that has triggered but not yet left the stack — [704.5v].)

2) Object type. While it is on the battlefield as Invasion of Ixalan, the permanent is a Battle — Siege ([Battle], [205.3q], [310.11]), not a creature, and only creatures can be sacrificed to that mode. Battles and creatures are distinct object types for combat and damage purposes ([506.3f], [506.3g], [120.1a]).

What Alondra can sacrifice: a creature they control at that time — for example Rankle and Torbran itself, if it's their only creature. The mode says each player sacrifices a creature of their choice, so with more than two players every player at the table sacrifices one, not just one opponent; with two players it's just the two of you.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Rankle and Torbran's damage trigger and the defeated trigger are put on the stack together after combat damage, and that Rankle and Torbran's trigger is resolved first or at least before Invasion of Ixalan is exiled and cast. If instead Alondra somehow let Invasion of Ixalan's defeated trigger fully resolve (exiling it and casting it transformed) and Belligerent Regisaur were already on the battlefield before Rankle and Torbran's ability resolved, then Belligerent Regisaur would be a legal creature to sacrifice — but that ordering isn't possible here, since Rankle and Torbran's ability is already on the stack above/alongside it and modal choices plus the sacrifice occur on its resolution.

Also relevant: Belligerent Regisaur's "whenever you cast a spell, this creature gains indestructible" would not help anyway, since sacrificing is not destruction ([701.21a]).

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. When Rankle and Torbran attacks Invasion of Ixalan and removes the last defense counter from it, both Invasion of Ixalan and Rankle and Torbran's abilities will trigger. Alondra will get to choose the order in which the abilities go on the stack, so they could put Rankle and Torbran's triggered ability on the stack first with Invasion of Ixalan's triggered ability on top. Invasion of Ixalan's triggered ability will resolve first, so Invasion of Ixalan will be exiled and Alondra could choose to cast it transformed. When Rankle and Torbran's triggered ability resolves, Belligerent Regisaur will have resolved and be on the battlefield, so Alondra could choose to sacrifice it.

If you'd rather not rely on ordering, Noah can simply let the sacrifice happen.
- Thespian's Stage remains tapped from paying the activation cost; becoming a copy doesn't untap it [Thespian's Stage ruling #2], and the copy effect lasts with no duration until it leaves the battlefield or another copy effect overwrites it, and it loses the "{T}: Add {C}" ability but keeps the copy ability by the "except it has this ability" clause [Thespian's Stage ruling #0].
