entries.question: Ashley controls [Underworld Breach] and has [Reveillark] in their graveyard. Can they evoke it?
entries.reason: Both the candidate and reference conclude escape and evoke are mutually exclusive alternative costs and that Underworld Breach's escape must be used to cast Reveillark from the graveyard, so its evoke cost cannot be paid.
entries.answer:
No. Ashley can cast Reveillark from their graveyard, but only for its escape cost — not for its evoke cost.

Why: Underworld Breach grants each nonland card in Ashley's graveyard escape, and escape is a static ability that says "You may cast this card from your graveyard by paying [cost] rather than paying its mana cost" — an alternative cost [702.138a]. Evoke is likewise an alternative cost: "You may cast this spell by paying [cost] rather than paying its mana cost" [702.74a]. Rule 601.2b states plainly that a player can't apply two alternative methods of casting or two alternative costs to a single spell. Escape is the only thing permitting Reveillark to be cast from the graveyard here, so escape's cost is the one Ashley must use, and evoke's {5}{W} can't be substituted on top of it [601.2b, 601.2f].

So the cost to cast Reveillark from the graveyard is Underworld Breach's escape cost: Reveillark's mana cost, {4}{W} (four generic plus one white), plus exiling three other cards from Ashley's graveyard as an additional part of that cost.

Consequence: because Ashley did not choose to pay Reveillark's evoke cost, evoke's triggered sacrifice ability does not trigger when Reveillark enters the battlefield — that trigger depends on the controller having chosen to pay the evoke cost [Reveillark ruling #5]. Reveillark simply stays on the battlefield, and its "when this creature leaves the battlefield" ability is available later [Reveillark ruling #6].

Timing note: evoke doesn't change when you may cast Reveillark [Reveillark ruling #0], so as a creature spell it's still cast only when Ashley could cast a sorcery — during their own main phase with an empty stack.

Nothing here depends on the number of players; the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Escape and evoke are both alternative costs ([702.138a], [702.74a]), and Ashley may only pay one alternative cost for a spell. Since escape is the only thing that allows Ashley to cast Reveillark from their graveyard, they have to use that cost.

entries.question: Autumn controls [Slimefoot, the Stowaway] and a 1/1 Saproling token. Autumn casts [Deafening Clarion] choosing both modes. How much life does Autumn gain?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Autumn gains two life in a two-player game—Slimefoot's death triggers its ability for 1 life and, because it had lifelink as it died, that 1 damage also causes an additional 1 life.
entries.answer:
Autumn gains 2 life in a two-player game (and more at a multiplayer table — see below).

Step by step:

1. Deafening Clarion's modes resolve in the order printed, so the 3 damage to each creature happens *before* Autumn's creatures gain lifelink. That means the damage Deafening Clarion itself deals gains Autumn no life at all — the creatures didn't have lifelink at the moment that damage was dealt. Deafening Clarion is also not Autumn's source of lifelink damage; it's a spell, and the lifelink is granted to creatures.

2. The 3 damage kills both the 1/1 Saproling token and Slimefoot, the Stowaway (a 2/3). Per [Deafening Clarion ruling #1], both are still on the battlefield to gain lifelink from the second mode before they die, so Slimefoot, the Stowaway does have lifelink when it dies.

3. The Saproling token dying triggers Slimefoot, the Stowaway's ability (it was on the battlefield as the token died): "Slimefoot deals 1 damage to each opponent and you gain 1 life." That's 1 life from the ability's own text.

4. That 1 damage to each opponent is dealt by Slimefoot, the Stowaway, which had lifelink as of last known information, so it also causes Autumn to gain that much life (702.15b, 120.3f). In a two-player game that's 1 more life.

Total in a two-player game: 1 (ability) + 1 (lifelink on the 1 damage) = 2 life. These are separate life-gain events (119.9, 702.15e), which matters for triggers like Ajani's Pridemate.

With more than two players: the ability still gives exactly 1 life once, but Slimefoot, the Stowaway deals 1 damage to each opponent, so lifelink gains 1 life per opponent. With three opponents Autumn gains 3 + 1 = 4 life.

Timing note: if a table instead resolved the lifelink mode before the damage mode, the 3 damage from Deafening Clarion would still not be lifelinked (Deafening Clarion is the source of that damage, not Autumn's creatures), so the answer would be unchanged.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold:
Two.

Deafening Clarion deals three damage to each creature, then gives them lifelink. After the spell has resolved, state-based actions are checked and both creatures die. Slimefoot, the Stowaway's ability is a leave-the-battlefield trigger, so it sees that it existed immediately before Slimefoot, the Stowaway died and therefore triggers. When it resolves, it sees that Slimefoot, the Stowaway had lifelink right before it died, so Autumn gains 1 life from the damage that's dealt to Noor.

entries.question: Ace controls [Soul Warden] and casts [Realmwalker]. Can Natalie kill it before Ace casts a creature from the top of their library?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude there is a priority window when Realmwalker enters (with Soul Warden's trigger on the stack) during which Natalie can respond with an instant to destroy Realmwalker and prevent Ace from gaining the permission to cast creatures off the top.
entries.answer:
Yes — Natalie can kill Realmwalker first, as long as she has an instant-speed way to do so.

Why: Ace can only cast a creature spell off the top of the library at normal timing — during Ace's main phase with the stack empty (Realmwalker doesn't change when creature spells can be cast; see [Realmwalker ruling #3]). Realmwalker itself has to resolve first, and Soul Warden's "Whenever another creature enters, you gain 1 life" ability triggers when Realmwalker enters and is put on the stack the next time a player would receive priority [117.2a]. For that trigger (and Realmwalker's own spell before it) to resolve, all players must pass in succession [608.1], which means Natalie receives priority and may respond with an instant or activated ability at that time [117.7]. So there is guaranteed to be a window in which Natalie holds priority with Realmwalker on the battlefield before Ace's stack is empty for a sorcery-timing creature spell.

If Natalie destroys Realmwalker in that window, Ace loses the permission and can't cast the creature card off the top: a player may begin casting a spell only if a rule or effect allows it [601.3], and the alternative-permission check happens when casting begins [601.3e].

One timing caveat: if Natalie waits until after Ace has already begun/finished casting the creature spell from the top of the library, killing Realmwalker does nothing to that spell — legality was checked as casting began, and the spell became cast and stays on the stack [601.2a], [601.2i]. It is not "undone" ([733.1] applies only to actions that were illegal or couldn't be completed). So Natalie should act while Realmwalker's enters-trigger from Soul Warden (or Realmwalker's own spell) is still on the stack, or in Ace's main phase before Ace casts.

Multiplayer: the same answer holds. With more than two players, every opponent gets priority in turn order before the stack empties, so any of them — not just Natalie — could remove Realmwalker in that window.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. When Realmwalker enters the battlefield Soul Warden's trigger will go on the stack, at which point both players will have a chance to respond.

entries.question: Alondra has 10 life and Nico has 20 life. Alondra attacks Nico with [Kaalia of the Vast] and puts in [Scourge of the Throne]. Will they get an extra combat phase?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude no — Scourge of the Throne's attack-trigger only triggers when it's declared as an attacker, and being put onto the battlefield already attacking does not count as being declared.
entries.answer:
No — Alondra does not get an additional combat phase from Scourge of the Throne in this situation.

Why: Kaalia of the Vast's triggered ability puts Scourge of the Throne onto the battlefield already tapped and attacking Nico; Scourge of the Throne is never declared as an attacker. Scourge of the Throne's ability is an "attacks" trigger with an intervening "if" clause, and the official ruling for it states the condition must hold "both when it's declared as an attacker and as it starts to resolve" — a creature that was put onto the battlefield attacking was never declared as an attacker, so that ability doesn't trigger and gives neither the untap nor the extra combat phase [Scourge of the Throne ruling #2]. Its dethrone ability likewise depends on attacking, and the same lack of an attack declaration is why it doesn't apply.

Note that the life totals wouldn't have been the obstacle: Nico at 20 life does have the most life among the players mentioned, so if Scourge of the Throne had actually been declared attacking Nico, both the dethrone counter and the untap-plus-extra-combat-phase effect would have applied, and the extra phase would be added directly after the current combat phase (the game then proceeds to that new combat phase rather than skipping ahead) [500.10], [505.1].

Multiplayer note: nothing here changes between a two-player game and a larger table except which player counts as having the most life — with more than two players, "the player with the most life or tied for most life" is measured across all players, and Kaalia of the Vast's creature enters attacking the opponent Kaalia attacked [Kaalia of the Vast ruling #1].

I'm assuming the standard sequence: attackers declared, Kaalia of the Vast's trigger resolves during the declare attackers step, and Scourge of the Throne enters at that point. If instead Scourge of the Throne had been on the battlefield untapped and been declared as an attacker against Nico normally, the answer flips and Alondra would get the extra combat phase.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Scourge of the Throne has a triggered ability that occurs only when it is declared as an attacking creature. It was put onto the battlefield attacking, which doesn't meet its trigger condition.

entries.question: Alma deals combat damage to Nico with their [Ragavan, Nimble Pilferer]. They exile [Deceit] from Nico's library. Can Alma evoke Deceit?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Ragavan's effect permits casting Deceit from exile and that evoke is an alternative cost that can be used when casting it from exile.
entries.answer:
Yes. Ragavan, Nimble Pilferer's ability says "Until end of turn, you may cast that card," which is permission to cast Deceit from exile, and evoke is an alternative cost that works from any zone Deceit can be cast from. So Alma may cast Deceit from exile for its evoke cost of {U/B}{U/B} (two mana, each either blue or black) instead of its {4}{U/B}{U/B} mana cost, provided Alma casts it before end of turn and at a legal time for a creature spell (their main phase with an empty stack, since Deceit is a creature spell with no flash).

Details:
- Evoke is two abilities: a static ability that functions in any zone from which the card can be cast, meaning "You may cast this card by paying [cost] rather than paying its mana cost," plus a triggered ability "When this permanent enters, if its evoke cost was paid, its controller sacrifices it" [702.74a]. Because the static half works in whatever zone the card can be cast from, it works in exile once Ragavan, Nimble Pilferer's effect grants permission to cast Deceit from there.
- Alma announces the evoke alternative cost as part of casting, following the alternative-cost rules [601.2b], and the total cost {U/B}{U/B} is locked in [601.2f]. The Treasure token Ragavan, Nimble Pilferer created can help pay it, since Treasure produces one mana of any color and each {U/B} can be paid with blue or black.
- Because the evoke cost was paid, Deceit enters the battlefield under Alma's control and is then sacrificed by the evoke trigger. Its enter triggers still happen: if {U}{U} was spent, Alma returns up to one other target nonland permanent to its owner's hand; if {B}{B} was spent, a target opponent reveals their hand and Alma chooses a nonland card to be discarded. Deceit's rulings confirm those abilities look at what mana was spent on the total cost, not just on the hybrid symbols [Deceit ruling #0] — so paying {U/B}{U/B} as {U}{U} or {B}{B} turns on the corresponding trigger.
- Note Alma can't combine evoke with another alternative casting method; only one alternative cost may apply to a spell [601.2b].

This works the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table; the only multiplayer wrinkle is that Deceit's black trigger targets an opponent, and Alma chooses which opponent — it need not be Nico.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Ragavan, Nimble Pilferer's trigger creates a continuous effect that lets Alma cast Deceit this turn, with no restrictions on how it's cast. Alma is free to cast Deceit for its alternative cost by evoking it.

entries.question: Amiyah taps their [The One Ring], which currently has no burden counters on it, to draw a card. Before that resolves Nico casts [Soul Partition] targeting The One Ring. How many cards does Amiyah draw when the activated ability resolves?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same ruling as the reference: the ring is exiled so no burden counter can be placed, last known information shows zero burdens, and Amiyah draws zero cards.
entries.answer:
Amiyah draws zero cards.

The activated ability of The One Ring exists on the stack independently of The One Ring, so exiling The One Ring with Soul Partition does not counter the ability — it still resolves [113.7a], [603.3]. The ability isn't targeted, so target-legality checks don't apply here [608.2b].

On resolution, the controller follows the instructions in order [608.2c]. First, "Put a burden counter on The One Ring" — The One Ring is no longer on the battlefield (it's in exile), so no counter can be put on it; that part simply does nothing. Then "draw a card for each burden counter on The One Ring" — since the object is no longer in the zone it's expected to be in, its last known information is used [113.7a], and its last known state was zero burden counters. Zero counters means zero cards drawn. The ability then finishes resolving and ceases to exist [608.2n].

Timing note: I'm assuming Soul Partition resolves (exiling The One Ring) before the tap ability resolves, as stated. If instead the tap ability had resolved first, The One Ring would still be on the battlefield, would get its first burden counter, and Amiyah would draw 1 card; Soul Partition exiling it afterward wouldn't undo that draw.

Nothing here depends on the number of players — the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table. (Soul Partition's "costs {2} more" clause only matters later, if Nico's opponent Amiyah chooses to play The One Ring from exile: it would then cost {4} plus {2} more, i.e. {6} generic.)

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: None. When The One Ring's ability resolves it can't put a burden counter on The One Ring because it's no longer on the battlefield. The game uses its last known information to determine how many burden counters were on The One Ring before it was exiled.

entries.question: Nathaniel controls [Rest in Peace] and [Dauthi Voidwalker], and Armani casts [Read the Bones]. What happens to it?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same core ruling as the reference: Armani chooses which replacement effect applies, and Read the Bones is exiled (with or without a void counter depending on Armani's choice).
entries.answer:
Read the Bones resolves fully (Armani scries 2, draws two cards, loses 2 life), and then, instead of being put into Armani's graveyard, Read the Bones is exiled — and Armani, as the card's owner, chooses which of the two replacement effects does the exiling.

Why: Rest in Peace says "If a card or token would be put into a graveyard from anywhere, exile it instead," and Dauthi Voidwalker says "If a card would be put into an opponent's graveyard from anywhere, instead exile it with a void counter on it." Armani is an opponent of Nathaniel, so both replacement effects try to modify the same event (Read the Bones going to Armani's graveyard). A replacement effect watches for an event and replaces it [614.1]. When two or more replacement effects apply to the same event, the affected object's controller — or its owner if it has no controller — chooses one to apply; a card on the stack/in transit to a graveyard has no controller, so Armani (its owner) chooses [616.1], [616.1e], [400.6]. Neither effect is a self-replacement effect nor changes control of a permanent entering the battlefield, so no effect is forced to go first [616.1a], [616.1b], [614.15]. Once the chosen effect is applied, the process repeats with any still-applicable effects — but Read the Bones is now in exile, not headed to a graveyard, so the other effect simply does nothing [616.1], [614.7].

Practically, Armani will choose Rest in Peace: that exiles Read the Bones with no void counter, so Nathaniel can't later use Dauthi Voidwalker's sacrifice ability to cast it. If Armani chose Dauthi Voidwalker instead, Read the Bones would be exiled with a void counter and Nathaniel could tap and sacrifice Dauthi Voidwalker to play it that turn without paying its mana cost.

This works the same in a two-player or multiplayer game; the only multiplayer wrinkle is that if several players had to make such choices simultaneously, those choices are made in APNAP order [101.4]. Also note Dauthi Voidwalker only applies to cards headed to an opponent's graveyard, so at a bigger table it hits every opponent of Nathaniel, while Rest in Peace applies to everyone including Nathaniel.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Armani gets to choose which replacement effect applies to it. After applying that effect, it's no longer moving to the graveyard, so the other effect doesn't apply. It'll end up in exile either way, but Armani gets to choose whether it has a void counter on it.

entries.question: Aspen control [Pulmonic Sliver]. They cast [Dihada's Ploy], discarding [Dregscape Sliver] on resolution. Can Aspen put Dregscape Sliver on top of their library?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Pulmonic Sliver's replacement ability only applies to permanents on the battlefield, so a Sliver discarded from hand (via Dihada's Ploy) cannot be put on top of the library.
entries.answer:
No. Dregscape Sliver goes to Aspen's graveyard normally.

Pulmonic Sliver's granted ability reads "If this permanent would be put into a graveyard, you may put it on top of its owner's library instead." The word "this permanent" limits the replacement effect to objects on the battlefield — a permanent is a card on the battlefield, not a card in hand. Discarding Dregscape Sliver moves it from Aspen's hand to their graveyard, so it is never a permanent being put into a graveyard and the replacement effect never applies. The rulings on Pulmonic Sliver back this up: they describe the effect applying to Slivers that would "die" (that is, be put into a graveyard from the battlefield), including Pulmonic Sliver itself and other Slivers dying at the same time [Pulmonic Sliver ruling #2] [Pulmonic Sliver ruling #3]. Card text controls here, and it simply doesn't cover a discard.

Side notes: Dregscape Sliver landing in the graveyard is fine for its own purposes — while Dregscape Sliver is on the battlefield it grants unearth {2} to Sliver creature cards in your graveyard, but it does not grant unearth to itself from the graveyard, since it only grants the ability while it's on the battlefield [Dregscape Sliver ruling #2]. Also, Dihada's Ploy's life gain counts every card discarded this turn, including the Dregscape Sliver discarded during its own resolution [Dihada's Ploy ruling #0].

This answer doesn't depend on player count — it's the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Pulmonic Sliver's ability affects only Sliver permanents on the battlefield, and not Sliver cards in other zones.

entries.question: Arely controls a [Barony Vampire]. Nico controls a [Trained Jackal]. Arely casts [Prey Upon], targeting the Barony Vampire and Trained Jackal. In response, Nico casts [Hanabi Blast], targeting the Barony Vampire. What happens?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Hanabi Blast destroys Barony Vampire before Prey Upon resolves, leaving an illegal target so Prey Upon does not cause any fight damage.
entries.answer:
Hanabi Blast resolves first and kills Barony Vampire; then Prey Upon resolves but no fight damage is dealt at all — Trained Jackal takes nothing.

Step by step:

1. Nico cast Hanabi Blast in response, so it's on top of the stack and resolves before Prey Upon [117.7]. It deals 2 damage to Barony Vampire, which is a 3/2, so lethal damage destroys it. Hanabi Blast then returns to its owner's hand (Nico's, since Nico owns and cast it) and Nico discards a card at random [Hanabi Blast ruling #0].

2. Prey Upon then tries to resolve. On resolution it rechecks its targets; a target that is no longer in the zone it was in when targeted is illegal, so Barony Vampire (now in the graveyard) is an illegal target [608.2b], [Illegal Target]. Trained Jackal is still a legal target, so Prey Upon isn't removed from the stack as having all illegal targets, but the fight simply does nothing: per Prey Upon's ruling, if either target is illegal as Prey Upon resolves, no creature deals or is dealt damage [Prey Upon ruling #0]. Trained Jackal survives untouched.

"Fight" means each of the two targeted creatures deals damage equal to its power to the other; it needs both creatures present, which is why losing one shuts the whole effect off.

Timing note: I'm assuming Hanabi Blast was cast after Prey Upon was already on the stack (as stated) and thus resolved first. If instead Hanabi Blast had somehow resolved after Prey Upon, Prey Upon would have resolved with both targets legal — Barony Vampire and Trained Jackal would have fought (Trained Jackal dying to 3 damage, Barony Vampire taking 1) — and Hanabi Blast's 2 damage would come afterward.

This analysis doesn't depend on player count: it works the same at a two-player table or a multiplayer table, since Prey Upon and Hanabi Blast each target specific objects rather than choosing among opponents.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: The Hanabi Blast resolves, removing the Barony Vampire from the battlefield. Prey Upon resolves, but no damage is dealt to the Trained Jackal.

entries.question: Annabel controls [Altar of Dementia] and casts [Too Greedily, Too Deep] returning Nolan's [Sepulchral Primordial] to the battlefield. Can Annabel use Altar of Dementia to sacrifice Sepulchral Primordial and return it to the battlefield using its own triggered ability?
entries.reason: The candidate gives the same final ruling and core reasoning: the Primordial's ETB trigger locks targets as it's put on the stack while the creature is still on the battlefield, so it cannot target or reanimate itself.
entries.answer:
No. Annabel cannot get Sepulchral Primordial to reanimate itself.

Why: Sepulchral Primordial's ability is a triggered ability that triggers when it enters the battlefield, and its targets ("up to one target creature card from that player's graveyard") are chosen at the time the triggered ability is put onto the stack, not when it resolves [113.7a]. At that moment Sepulchral Primordial is on the battlefield under Annabel's control (Too Greedily, Too Deep put it there), so it is not a creature card in any graveyard and is not a legal target for its own ability. No player receives priority in between the trigger event and the trigger being put on the stack with targets locked in, so Annabel has no window to sacrifice Sepulchral Primordial to Altar of Dementia first.

If Annabel instead activates Altar of Dementia after the trigger is already on the stack, sacrificing Sepulchral Primordial only puts it into Nolan's graveyard (it's Nolan's card) — the ability on the stack still has whatever other targets were chosen, and it never had Sepulchral Primordial as a target, so it won't return it. Zone-change triggered abilities like this look for objects only in the specified zone as chosen/resolved, and a card that changes zones becomes a new object with no relation to its former existence [603.6][400.7].

What Annabel can do: when Sepulchral Primordial's trigger is put on the stack, she may choose up to one target creature card in each opponent's graveyard — including Nolan's graveyard — and reanimate those under her control. In a two-player game that's one target (from Nolan's graveyard); at a multiplayer table she gets one potential target per opponent, so more creatures can come back [101.4 covers the general multiplayer choice ordering].

Timing note: I'm assuming Too Greedily, Too Deep fully resolved (including Sepulchral Primordial dealing damage equal to its power to each other creature) before the enters-the-battlefield trigger goes on the stack, which is how it must work. If Sepulchral Primordial somehow left the battlefield before its trigger was put on the stack, the trigger would still go on the stack and still could not target the card in the graveyard, because targets are locked in at that point and the ability was already on its way with no legal chance to name itself.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Annabel must choose a target for Sepulchral Primordial's triggered ability as it is put onto the stack. At this time, Sepulchral Primordial is still on the battlefield.

entries.question: Ari casts [Memories Returning]. Does Noor have a chance to exile it with [Dawnhand Dissident] before Ari can cast Memories Returning again for its flashback cost?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Noor cannot exile Memories Returning before Ari can flashback it because Ari receives priority immediately after it resolves and can cast it from the graveyard, with only the same noted exceptions.
entries.answer:
No — assuming Memories Returning resolved on Ari's turn and Ari can pay the flashback cost right away, Noor never gets a window to exile it with Dawnhand Dissident.

Why: when Memories Returning finishes resolving it's put into Ari's graveyard, and after a spell resolves the active player (Ari) receives priority first [608.1]. Since Memories Returning is a sorcery, Ari may recast it via flashback only during their own main phase with an empty stack [117.1a], [702.34a], [Memories Returning ruling #0] — and that is exactly the moment Ari holds priority. Flashback means "you may cast this card from your graveyard by paying {7}{U}{U} rather than its mana cost," and the card is exiled instead of going anywhere else when it leaves the stack [702.34a], [Memories Returning ruling #3]. The relevant ruling is explicit: if a card with flashback is put into your graveyard during your turn, you can cast it if it's legal to do so before any other player can take any actions [Memories Returning ruling #2]. Once Ari has moved Memories Returning from the graveyard to the stack, it's a spell, not a graveyard card, so Dawnhand Dissident's "{T}, Blight 2: Exile target card from a graveyard" has no legal target on it [112.1], [601.2a].

When Noor *can* get it: Dawnhand Dissident's exile ability is an activated ability Noor can only use with priority [117.1a]. So if Ari can't or doesn't cast Memories Returning immediately and instead passes priority, Noor may then activate Dawnhand Dissident (tapping it and paying Blight 2) to exile Memories Returning from Ari's graveyard, and Ari loses the flashback option. Likewise, Noor can pre-emptively hold up Dawnhand Dissident, but there's no point in the sequence where Noor gets priority between Memories Returning hitting the graveyard and Ari's flashback cast. Note also that if Noor activates Dawnhand Dissident targeting Memories Returning while it's still in the graveyard and Ari had already passed, Ari could not respond by flashing it back, since a sorcery can't be cast with something on the stack [117.1a], [117.7].

Timing assumption: I read this as Memories Returning being cast from hand, resolving, and going to the graveyard during Ari's main phase. If instead Memories Returning ended up in Ari's graveyard at some other time (say during someone else's turn, or countered while other players held priority), Noor would have normal priority windows to exile it before Ari's next main phase.

Multiplayer: the answer is the same with more than two players — the active player still receives priority first after a spell resolves, so no opponent gets in between [608.1], [117.1a].

entries.answer_gold:
No. After Memories Returning resolves, Ari receives priority.. At this point, Memories Returning is in the graveyard, and they can choose to cast it again. When it's cast, it goes from the graveyard to the stack. Noor does not receive priority until after Memories Returning is on the stack, so Memories Returning can't be exiled with Dawnhand Dissident.

(Unless there's something else on the battlefield that would create a triggered ability when Memories Returning resolves. In that case, Ari wouldn't be able to cast Memories Returning until the trigger has left the stack, and Noor could exile it in response to the trigger.)

entries.question: Aubrey and Arely are playing 2HG. Aubrey attacks with [Coral Commando] and Arely casts [Flash Conscription] to gain control of Coral Commando after it's been declared as an attacker in the declare attackers step. Is it still attacking?
entries.reason: Both answers reach the same conclusion that when Arely gains control of Coral Commando it changes controller and is removed from combat, so it is no longer attacking.
entries.answer:
No — Coral Commando stops being an attacking creature the moment Flash Conscription resolves and Arely gains control of it.

Why: a permanent is removed from combat if its controller changes, and a creature removed from combat stops being an attacking, blocking, blocked, and/or unblocked creature [506.4a]. Flash Conscription reads "Untap target creature and gain control of it until end of turn," so control of Coral Commando moves from Aubrey to Arely, which is exactly a control change. This is true whether Arely is Aubrey's Two-Headed Giant teammate or an opposing player — the rule keys off the controller changing, not off team membership. In shared-team-turns games the attacking team still declares attackers individually per creature and the team's attack must be legal as a whole [805.10b], but that doesn't stop the later control change from pulling Coral Commando out of combat.

A few knock-on points:
- Removing Coral Commando from combat happens without Aubrey's declaration being undone. Coral Commando was still legally declared as an attacker, so any "whenever a creature attacks" abilities that already triggered at declaration stay triggered [508.2a], and Aubrey's team is still considered to have "attacked" that defending player for effects that check that [508.6].
- Coral Commando is no longer attacking, so it deals no combat damage in the combat damage step and can't be blocked.
- Flash Conscription does not put Coral Commando back into combat; nothing in its text states the creature is attacking, which is what rules like [508.4] would require to make a creature attacking outside the declare attackers step.

Timing assumption: I'm reading this as Flash Conscription resolving after attackers were declared, during the declare attackers step. If instead Flash Conscription had resolved before attackers were declared, Arely would simply be able to declare Coral Commando as an attacker (it has haste), and it would be attacking normally.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. A creature that changes controllers is removed from combat. Even though Aubrey and Arely are on the same team and are both allowed to be attacking with creatures, they are different players and therefore Arely gaining control of Aubrey's creature still qualifies as a control change.

entries.question: Axel controls [Vastwood Gorger] and attacks Nico's [Teferi, Who Slows the Sunset]. Before damage is dealt, Nico activates [Barrin, Master Wizard], sacrificing Teferi, Who Slows the Sunset. Does Vastwood Gorger deal damage? If so, to what?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same conclusion that Vastwood Gorger deals no combat damage because it is no longer attacking anything (and cannot trample to the player).
entries.answer:
Vastwood Gorger deals no combat damage at all.

When Teferi, Who Slows the Sunset is sacrificed, it leaves the battlefield and is therefore removed from combat [506.4c]. Vastwood Gorger, however, is not removed from combat — removing the planeswalker being attacked doesn't remove the attacking creature. Vastwood Gorger continues to be an attacking creature, but it isn't attacking any player, planeswalker, or battle, and it may still be blocked; if it's unblocked it deals no combat damage [506.4c].

In the combat damage step, an unblocked creature assigns its damage to the player, planeswalker, or battle it's attacking; if it isn't currently attacking anything (for example, the planeswalker it was attacking left the battlefield), it assigns no combat damage [510.1b]. Vastwood Gorger has no trample, so none of its damage can be shifted to Nico — a creature without "trample over planeswalkers" that was attacking a planeswalker can't assign any combat damage to the defending player even if that planeswalker was removed from combat [702.19f]. (The trample exception in [702.19e] applies only to creatures with trample over planeswalkers, which Vastwood Gorger doesn't have.)

So Nico takes 0 damage and Vastwood Gorger simply sits there attacking nothing. Note also that Nico's Barrin, Master Wizard ability returns a target creature to its owner's hand; if Nico instead targeted Vastwood Gorger with it, Vastwood Gorger would leave the battlefield and be removed from combat [506.4c] — also dealing no damage.

Timing assumption: this all happens before the combat damage step, as stated. If somehow the sacrifice happened after combat damage was already dealt, the damage to Teferi, Who Slows the Sunset would already have been dealt and the sacrifice would change nothing about it.

This outcome is the same whether the game has two players or more than two — the attacked planeswalker's controller is the defending player [508.5], and no multiplayer rule provided changes the damage assignment here.

entries.answer_gold: No, Vastwood Gorger does not deal any combat damage. When combat damage would be assigned, a creature that is not currently attacking anything does not deal combat damage.
